vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: Doing something ‘just ONE time UNDER’ (下) makes it quick and easy.
vocabulary.etymology: 一下 is a numeral-classifier phrase meaning ‘one instance’. Adding 儿 (ér) is a northern Mandarin colloquial suffix.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ děng wǒ yīxiàr.
examples.english: Wait for me a sec.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kàn yīxiàr càidān.
examples.english: Let me take a look at the menu.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Softens requests and commands, making them sound more polite. Often used after verbs (V+一下儿).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘ONE’ (一) handful of ‘THESE’ (些) things.
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 些, where 些 originally depicted two piles of earth, representing ‘plurality’ or ‘many’.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mǎile yīxiē shuǐguǒ.
examples.english: I bought some fruit.

examples.pinyin: Zhèlǐ yǒu yīxiē wèntí.
examples.english: There are some problems here.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for uncountable nouns or plural countable nouns. Less vague than ‘一点’.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: Just ‘ONE’ (一) small ‘MEETING’ (会) of time.
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 会儿, where 会 (huì) means ‘to gather’ or ‘a moment’.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yīhuìr jiù lái.
examples.english: I'll be there in a moment.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen zuò yīhuìr ba.
examples.english: Let's sit for a while.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Common in northern speech with 儿化音 (érhuà). Can mean ‘soon’ or ‘a short time’.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Picture cutting something into ‘ONE’ (一) ‘HALF’ (半).
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 半, where 半 depicts splitting an ox in two, meaning ‘half’.

examples.pinyin: Zhège dàngāo wǒ chī yībàn.
examples.english: I'll eat half of this cake.

examples.chinese: 一半人同意，一半人不同意。
examples.pinyin: Yībàn rén tóngyì, yībàn rén bù tóngyì.
examples.english: Half the people agree, half don't.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Directly modifies nouns (e.g., 一半苹果). Can be used as a subject or object.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘ONE’ (一) ‘PIECE’ (块) — we are one piece/group.
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 块儿, where 块 is a classifier for lumps or pieces, implying unity.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen yīkuàir qù chīfàn ba.
examples.english: Let's go eat together.

examples.pinyin: Tāmen cóngxiǎo yīkuàir zhǎngdà.
examples.english: They grew up together since childhood.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Colloquial northern equivalent of 一起 (yīqǐ). Often used in spoken Chinese.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘ONE’ (一) ‘APPEARANCE’ (样) — they look one and the same.
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 样 (yàng), where 样 means ‘appearance’ or ‘kind’.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen liǎ de shǒujī yīyàng.
examples.english: Our phones are the same.

examples.chinese: 这个和那个味道一样吗？
examples.pinyin: Zhège hé nàgè wèidào yīyàng ma?
examples.english: Does this taste the same as that?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used with 跟/和...一样 (gēn/hé ... yīyàng) to mean ‘the same as...’. Can also be an adjective alone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: Just ‘ONE’ (一) tiny ‘DOT’ (点) of something.
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 点儿, where 点 originally depicted a black dot, meaning ‘a speck’.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào yīdiǎnr shuǐ.
examples.english: I want a little water.

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān yǒu yīdiǎnr lěng.
examples.english: It's a bit cold today.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for uncountable nouns or to soften adjectives (adj+一点儿). Northern colloquial with 儿化音.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘ONE’ (一) ‘SIDE’ (边) of the story, or doing two things side-by-side.
vocabulary.etymology: 一 (one) + 边 (biān), where 边 means ‘side’ or ‘edge’.

examples.pinyin: Tā zuò zài wǒ yībiān.
examples.english: He sat on my side.

examples.chinese: 我一边吃饭，一边看电视。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ yībiān chīfàn, yībiān kàn diànshì.
examples.english: I eat while watching TV.

vocabulary.usage_notes: As a noun: ‘one side’. As an adverb: used duplicated (一边...一边...) to mean ‘while doing A, also doing B’.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO UP’ (上) to the place of ‘LEARNING’ (学).
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (to go up/to attend) + 学 (to study/learning). Historically, attending school was seen as an elevated activity.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ dìdi qī suì shàngxué.
examples.english: My younger brother started school at seven.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ měitiān zěnme shàngxué?
examples.english: How do you get to school every day?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to the general act of attending school, not a specific class. Often used for students.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: The ‘TIME’ (次) that was ‘ABOVE/BEFORE’ (上) this one.
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (upper/previous) + 次 (time/instance). 上 here indicates ‘previous in sequence’.

examples.pinyin: Shàngcì wǒmen jiànguò.
examples.english: We met last time.

examples.pinyin: Shàngcì de zuòyè hěn nán.
examples.english: Last time's homework was hard.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to the most recent past occurrence of a repeated event.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO UP’ (上) to your ‘SHIFT’ (班).
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (to go up/to attend) + 班 (shift/class). 班 originally meant ‘to divide jade’, later extended to ‘work shift’.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bàba jiǔ diǎn shàngbān.
examples.english: My dad goes to work at nine.

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān bùyòng shàngbān.
examples.english: No work tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for starting a work shift, not just ‘to work’ in a general sense.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO UP’ (上) onto the ‘NET’ (网).
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (to go up/board) + 网 (wǎng, net). A modern compound for entering the internet/net.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan shàngwǎng kàn diànyǐng.
examples.english: I like to go online to watch movies.

examples.pinyin: Zhèlǐ kěyǐ shàngwǎng ma?
examples.english: Can I get online here?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Colloquial for browsing the internet, using social media, etc.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO UP’ (上) to the ‘CLASS’ (课).
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (to go up/to attend) + 课 (kè, lesson). 课 originally meant ‘to test’, later ‘lesson’.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bā diǎn shàngkè.
examples.english: We have class at eight.

examples.pinyin: Lǎoshī láile, kuài shàngkè!
examples.english: The teacher's here, class is starting!

vocabulary.usage_notes: For both students (‘to attend class’) and teachers (‘to teach a class’).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO UP’ (上) into the ‘VEHICLE’ (车).
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (to go up/board) + 车 (chē, vehicle). A straightforward compound for boarding.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng dàjiā páiduì shàngchē.
examples.english: Please line up to get on the bus.

examples.pinyin: Kuài diǎnr, yào shàngchē le!
examples.english: Hurry up, we need to get on!

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for buses, cars, trains, etc. Opposite is 下车 (xià chē).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: The ‘SIDE’ (边) that is ‘UP’ (上).
vocabulary.etymology: 上 (up) + 边 (side/edge). A compound indicating location.

examples.pinyin: Shū zài zhuōzi shàngbian.
examples.english: The book is on top of the table.

examples.pinyin: Kàn tú shàngbian de zì.
examples.english: Look at the words above the picture.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Colloquial location word. 上边/上面 are interchangeable in speech.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: The ‘TIME’ (次) that is ‘UNDER/NEXT’ (下) in line.
vocabulary.etymology: 下 (lower/next) + 次 (time/instance). 下 here indicates ‘next in sequence’.

examples.pinyin: Xiàcì wǒ qǐngkè.
examples.english: Next time, it's my treat.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen xiàcì zài liáo.
examples.english: Let's chat again next time.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Common parting phrase. Refers to the immediate future occurrence.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO DOWN’ (下) from your ‘SHIFT’ (班).
vocabulary.etymology: 下 (to go down/disembark) + 班 (shift/class). Opposite of 上班.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jǐ diǎn xiàbān?
examples.english: What time do you get off work?

examples.pinyin: Xiàbān yǐhòu wǒ qù jiànshēnfáng.
examples.english: After work, I go to the gym.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to finishing a work shift. Often followed by 以后 (yǐhòu).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO DOWN’ (下) from the ‘CLASS’ (课).
vocabulary.etymology: 下 (to go down/finish) + 课 (lesson). Opposite of 上课.

examples.pinyin: Hái yǒu wǔ fēnzhōng jiù xiàkè le.
examples.english: Class will be over in five minutes.

examples.pinyin: Xiàkè yǐhòu nǐ qù nǎr?
examples.english: Where are you going after class?

vocabulary.usage_notes: For students and teachers. Can also be used as an exclamation: ‘下课了！’

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘GO DOWN’ (下) from the ‘VEHICLE’ (车).
vocabulary.etymology: 下 (to go down/disembark) + 车 (vehicle). Opposite of 上车.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ dào zhànle, gāi xiàchē le.
examples.english: I'm at my stop, I should get off.

examples.pinyin: Xiàchē qǐng dāngxīn.
examples.english: Please be careful when getting off.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for all vehicles. Often heard on public transport announcements.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: The ‘SIDE’ (边) that is ‘DOWN’ (下).
vocabulary.etymology: 下 (down) + 边 (side/edge). A compound indicating location.

examples.pinyin: Māo zài chuáng xiàbian.
examples.english: The cat is under the bed.

examples.pinyin: Dá'àn zài xiàbian.
examples.english: The answer is below.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Colloquial location word. 下边/下面 are interchangeable in speech.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: Water is ‘FALLING DOWN’ (下) from the sky as ‘RAIN’ (雨).
vocabulary.etymology: 下 (to fall) + 雨 (yǔ, rain). 雨 is a pictograph of rain falling from a cloud.

examples.pinyin: Hǎoxiàng yào xiàyǔ le.
examples.english: It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.pinyin: Zuótiān xiàle hěn dà de yǔ.
examples.english: It rained heavily yesterday.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A subjectless verb (no ‘it’). Often used with 了 (le) to indicate change of state.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘NOT’ (不) ‘BIG’ (大) = ‘not very’.
vocabulary.etymology: 不 (not) + 大 (big/large). A straightforward negation.

examples.pinyin: Zhège fángjiān bù dà.
examples.english: This room isn't big.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ duì tā bù dà liǎojiě.
examples.english: I don't know him very well.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can be literal (‘not big’) or used as an adverb to soften negatives (‘not very’).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘NOT’ (不) ‘CORRECT’ (对) = wrong.
vocabulary.etymology: 不 (not) + 对 (correct). 对 originally depicted a hand holding a tablet, implying ‘to correspond’.

examples.pinyin: Zhège dá'àn bùduì.
examples.english: This answer is incorrect.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ juéde yǒudiǎn bùduì.
examples.english: I feel something's not right.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can describe facts, situations, or feelings. More common in speech than 错误 (cuòwù).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think: ‘NOT’ (不) ‘NEED TO USE’ (用).
vocabulary.etymology: 不 (not) + 用 (to use). A common negation.

examples.pinyin: Bùyòng xiè.
examples.english: You're welcome. (No need to thank me.)

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān bùyòng dài shū.
examples.english: No need to bring the book tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A polite way to refuse or say something is unnecessary. Often pronounced quickly as ‘béng’ in northern speech.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like the sun (日) rising behind a tree (木) in the EAST.
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 東. The traditional form depicts the sun (日) rising through trees (木), indicating the direction of sunrise.

examples.pinyin: Tàiyang cóng dōngbian shēngqǐ.
examples.english: The sun rises in the east.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā zài chéng dōng.
examples.english: My home is in the east of the city.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used in compounds (东边, 东方) or place names (山东). One of the four cardinal directions.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Imagine the sun rising in the East and shining on one 'side' (边) of your house.
vocabulary.etymology: 东 (東) originally depicted the sun rising behind a tree (木). 边 (邊) signifies a border or side.

examples.pinyin: Chāo shì zài wǒ jiā dōng bian.
examples.english: The supermarket is to the east of my house.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men wǎng dōng bian zǒu zou ba.
examples.english: Let's walk towards the east side.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used with 在 (zài) to indicate location. The 边 (bian) is often pronounced in the neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of 'a couple' or 'a pair' of things you need to 'weigh' (sounds like liǎng).
vocabulary.etymology: Originally represented a pair of weights, hence its association with the number two and measurement.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào mǎi liǎng gè píng guǒ.
examples.english: I want to buy two apples.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men liǎng gè rén qù chī fàn.
examples.english: The two of us are going to eat.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for counting general items (followed by a measure word like 个). Use 二 for numbers, counting in sequence, or in decimals.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Picture a flagpole (丨) through the center of a box (口) — right in the MIDDLE.
vocabulary.etymology: The character depicts a flagpole or arrow piercing the center of a target or an enclosure, indicating centrality.

examples.pinyin: Zhuō zi zài fáng jiān de zhōng jiān.
examples.english: The table is in the middle of the room.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shì Zhōng guó rén.
examples.english: I am Chinese.

vocabulary.usage_notes: When meaning 'China' or 'Chinese', it's often capitalized in pinyin (Zhōng). As a standalone word, it often means 'middle'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The 'middle' (中) place of 'learning' (学) — between elementary and high school.
vocabulary.etymology: 中 (middle) + 学 (learning, school). Refers to the intermediate stage of education.

measure_word.example: 一所中学 (yì suǒ zhōng xué)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mèi mei zài shàng zhōng xué.
examples.english: My younger sister is in middle school.

examples.pinyin: Zhè suǒ zhōng xué hěn dà.
examples.english: This middle school is very big.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to secondary education in China, typically covering grades 7-12, but often used for junior high (7-9).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A person who is a 'middle school' (中学) 'life'/'born' (生) — a student born of middle school.
vocabulary.etymology: 中学 (middle school) + 生 (life, person born into a role). Literally 'middle school life-person'.

measure_word.example: 一个中学生 (yí gè zhōng xué shēng)

examples.pinyin: Zhè xiē zhōng xué shēng hěn máng.
examples.english: These middle school students are very busy.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ dì di shì zhōng xué shēng.
examples.english: My younger brother is a middle school student.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very common term for a young student. The 生 is often used to denote a person in a specific role (e.g., 医生 doctor, 学生 student).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The 'Chinese' (中) 'writing/language' (文) you are learning right now!
vocabulary.etymology: 中 (China) + 文 (writing, language, culture). The language/writing of China.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ huì shuō Zhōng wén ma?
examples.english: Can you speak Chinese?

examples.pinyin: Zhōng wén hěn yǒu yì si.
examples.english: Chinese is very interesting.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The most common term for the Chinese language. 汉语 is also common but slightly more formal/academic.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of being 'in the middle' of two things — '中' is the center point, '间' is the space in between.
vocabulary.etymology: 中 (center) + 间 (interval, space between). Refers to the central space or interval.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuò wǒ men zhōng jiān ba.
examples.english: Sit between us.

examples.pinyin: Zhào piàn zhōng jiān de rén shì wǒ.
examples.english: The person in the middle of the photo is me.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Specifically refers to the space between two or more points/objects, not just a general center area.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like a tall shelf with books on it. The sound 'shū' is like 'shush' in a library.
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 書, which depicts a hand (聿) holding a brush over a surface (曰), representing writing and thus a book.

examples.pinyin: Zhè běn shū hěn hǎo kàn.
examples.english: This book is very good to read.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ qù tú shū guǎn jiè shū.
examples.english: I'm going to the library to borrow books.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The universal word for book. Also appears in compounds related to writing and studying.

vocabulary.mnemonic: It's a 'bag' (包) specifically for your 'books' (书).
vocabulary.etymology: 书 (book) + 包 (bag, wrap). A bag for books.

measure_word.example: 一个书包 (yí gè shū bāo)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de shū bāo hěn zhòng.
examples.english: My backpack is very heavy.

examples.pinyin: Bié wàng le nǐ de shū bāo.
examples.english: Don't forget your schoolbag.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Almost exclusively refers to a student's backpack for carrying books, not a general-purpose bag.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A 'shop' (店) that sells 'books' (书).
vocabulary.etymology: 书 (book) + 店 (shop, store). A book shop.

measure_word.example: 一家书店 (yì jiā shū diàn)

examples.pinyin: Qián miàn yǒu yì jiā shū diàn.
examples.english: There's a bookstore ahead.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xǐ huan qù shū diàn.
examples.english: I like going to the bookstore.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very common word. Often combined with 去 (qù) 'go to' or 在 (zài) 'at'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of an official 'affair' with many lines of paperwork — the character has many strokes.
vocabulary.etymology: The original form depicted a hand holding a tool recording events on bamboo slips, representing affairs or events.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu shì, xiān zǒu le.
examples.english: I have something to do, I'm leaving first.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì xiǎo shì, méi guān xi.
examples.english: This is a small matter, it's okay.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Extremely common and versatile. Often used in phrases like 有事 (yǒu shì) 'busy/have matters' and 没事 (méi shì) 'it's nothing/I'm free'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The 'now' (今) 'year' (年). It's the year we are in right now.
vocabulary.etymology: 今 (now, this) + 年 (year). This current year.

examples.pinyin: Jīn nián wǒ shí bā suì.
examples.english: I am 18 years old this year.

examples.pinyin: Jīn nián xià tiān hěn rè.
examples.english: This summer is very hot.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Always placed at the beginning of a time phrase. Contrast with 今年 (jīn nián) and 明年 (míng nián).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like one person (人) following another (人), showing movement FROM one point TO another.
vocabulary.etymology: Depicts one person following another, indicating following, compliance, and by extension, a starting point (from).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ cóng Zhōng guó lái.
examples.english: I come from China.

examples.pinyin: Cóng míng tiān kāi shǐ.
examples.english: Starting from tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A fundamental preposition for stating origin or starting point in time/place. Often used in the pattern 从…到… (cóng... dào...) 'from... to...'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: It's '他' (he/him) plus '们' (plural marker). So, a group of hes/them.
vocabulary.etymology: 他 (he, him) + 们 (plural suffix for people).

examples.pinyin: Tā men shì wǒ de tóng xué.
examples.english: They are my classmates.

examples.pinyin: Tā men zài nǎr?
examples.english: Where are they?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for a group of all males or a mixed-gender group. For a group of all females, use 她们 (tā men).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Imagine leaning your body (休) against a tree and then sitting (息) down to take a break.
vocabulary.etymology: 休 (depicts a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木, to rest) + 息 (breath, to cease). To rest and catch one's breath.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ lèi le, xiǎng xiū xi yí xià.
examples.english: I'm tired, I want to rest for a bit.

examples.pinyin: Zhōng wǔ xiū xi yí gè xiǎo shí.
examples.english: There's a one-hour break at noon.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can be used as a verb or a noun (a rest/break). Often followed by 一下 (yí xià) or a time duration.

vocabulary.mnemonic: It's '你' (you) plus '们' (plural marker). So, 'you all'.
vocabulary.etymology: 你 (you, singular) + 们 (plural suffix for people).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ men hǎo!
examples.english: Hello (to all of you)!

examples.pinyin: Nǐ men yào qù nǎr?
examples.english: Where are you all going?

vocabulary.usage_notes: The standard plural 'you'. There's no distinction for formal/informal in the plural form.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of ONE (元 sounds like 'one') basic unit of Chinese money.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally meant 'head', 'chief', or 'first'. Extended to mean the primary unit, hence the basic monetary unit.

examples.pinyin: Zhè gè píng guǒ wǔ yuán.
examples.english: This apple is five yuan.

examples.pinyin: Gěi wǒ shí yuán.
examples.english: Give me ten yuan.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The formal name for the Chinese currency unit. In everyday speech, 块 (kuài) is more common. 1元 = 1块.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A person (儿) walking ahead on the road (一), going FIRST.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted a foot (止) ahead of a person (儿), indicating going ahead or being first.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiān qǐng.
examples.english: You go first (after you).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiān huí jiā.
examples.english: I'm going home first.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Placed before the verb to indicate an action is done first. Often used with 再 (zài) 'then' in the pattern 先…再… (first... then...).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Picture the two lines on top as a door lintel, and the bottom is the bolt — you slide it to CLOSE the door.
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 關, which depicted a bar or bolt across a gate.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng guān mén.
examples.english: Please close the door.

examples.pinyin: Guān dēng shuì jiào.
examples.english: Turn off the light and sleep.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for closing physical things (doors, windows) and turning off devices (lights, TV, computer). The opposite is 开 (kāi).

vocabulary.mnemonic: To 'close' (关) something and have it be 'up' (上) — implying the action is completed.
vocabulary.etymology: 关 (to close) + 上 (up, indicating completion or direction of the action).

examples.pinyin: Bǎ chuāng hu guān shàng.
examples.english: Close the window.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ shū guān shàng.
examples.english: Please close the book.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A verb-complement phrase where 上 indicates the action is done thoroughly or to completion. Very common in imperative sentences.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of doing something 'once more' — it happens 'again'.
vocabulary.etymology: Possibly derived from a pictograph of a fish, later borrowed for its sound to mean 'again'. Its original meaning is obscure.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn.
examples.english: Please say it again.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men míng tiān zài jiàn.
examples.english: See you again tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for a future repetition ('do something again'). 又 (yòu) is for past repetitions. Often used in polite requests.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The 冫 radical on the left means 'ice'. Things with ice are COLD.
vocabulary.etymology: Contains the 冫 (bīng) 'ice' radical, combined with a phonetic component. Directly relates to cold temperature.

examples.pinyin: Jīn tiān hěn lěng.
examples.english: It's very cold today.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shuǐ tài lěng le.
examples.english: This water is too cold.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Describes low temperature of weather, objects, or feelings (冷淡 lěngdàn). The opposite is 热 (rè).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Imagine a plant (屮) growing OUT of a pot or box (凵).
vocabulary.etymology: Depicts a foot stepping out of a cavity or enclosure, representing emergence or going out.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ chū qù yí xià.
examples.english: I'm going out for a bit.

examples.pinyin: Tài yáng chū lái le.
examples.english: The sun has come out.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A fundamental verb of motion. Often combined with direction complements like 去 (chū qù 'go out') and 来 (chū lái 'come out').

vocabulary.mnemonic: To 'exit' (出) and go 'away' (去) from where you are.
vocabulary.etymology: 出 (to exit) + 去 (to go away from the speaker).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men yì qǐ chū qù chī fàn ba.
examples.english: Let's go out to eat together.

examples.pinyin: Bié chū qù, zài xià yǔ.
examples.english: Don't go out, it's raining.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A directional verb complement phrase. The action moves away from the speaker. The opposite (moving towards) is 进来 (jìn lái).

vocabulary.mnemonic: To 'exit' (出) and come 'towards' (来) the speaker.
vocabulary.etymology: 出 (to exit) + 来 (to come towards the speaker).

examples.pinyin: Kuài chū lái, chē lái le!
examples.english: Come out quickly, the car is here!

examples.pinyin: Dá àn xiǎng chū lái le ma?
examples.english: Have you figured out the answer?

vocabulary.usage_notes: A directional verb complement phrase. The action moves towards the speaker or results in something becoming apparent.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think "BEE-yéah! Don't do that!"
vocabulary.etymology: Originally a combination of a knife (刂) and a bone, representing separation or cutting apart. Now means to leave, to differentiate, or used as a prohibitive particle.

examples.pinyin: Bié shuō huà le.
examples.english: Stop talking.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān bié chídào le.
examples.english: Let's not be late tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: As a verb, means to leave or separate. As a particle, used before a verb to express a negative command ("don't").

vocabulary.mnemonic: It's '别' (other/different) + '人' (person). The different person.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 别 (different/other) and 人 (person). Literally "different person" or "other person".

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì biéren de dōngxi.
examples.english: This belongs to someone else.

examples.pinyin: Bú yào zǒng gēn biéren bǐ.
examples.english: Don't always compare yourself to others.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 'ren' here is neutral tone. Refers to people other than oneself or the person being discussed.

vocabulary.mnemonic: "别的" sounds like "buy day" - go buy something else.
vocabulary.etymology: 别 (other/different) + 的 (possessive/adjectival particle). Literally "belonging to the other/ different category".

examples.pinyin: Nǐ hái yào hē diǎn biéde ma?
examples.english: Do you want to drink something else?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ méi bié de shì le.
examples.english: I have nothing else (to do).

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used to ask for or indicate alternatives. The 'de' is usually neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 前 (before) + 天 (day). The day before the current day (yesterday).
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 前 (before) and 天 (day). Literally "before day".

examples.pinyin: Wǒ qiántiān qù guàngjiē le.
examples.english: I went shopping the day before yesterday.

examples.pinyin: Qiántiān xiàyǔ le.
examples.english: It rained the day before yesterday.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 前 (front) + 边 (side). The side that's in front.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 前 (before/front) and 边 (side/edge). Literally "front side".

examples.pinyin: Tā jiā jiù zài chāoshì qiánbian.
examples.english: His house is right in front of the supermarket.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng wǎng qiánbian zǒu.
examples.english: Please walk ahead.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 'bian' here is neutral tone. A very common, casual way to say "in front".

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like a person (力) lifting a heavy weight (云) — you have to MOVE to do that.
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 動, which combines 重 (heavy) and 力 (force/strength), implying the exertion of force to move something heavy.

examples.pinyin: Bié dòng wǒ de diànnǎo!
examples.english: Don't touch/move my computer!

examples.pinyin: Wǒ lèi le, bù xiǎng dòng.
examples.english: I'm tired, I don't want to move.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very versatile verb. Can mean to move physically, to touch, to operate, or to act.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 动 (move) + 作 (make/do). The thing you make when you move.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 动 (to move) and 作 (to do/make). Literally "moving-doing".

examples.pinyin: Zhège wǔdǎo dòngzuò hěn nán.
examples.english: This dance move is very difficult.

examples.pinyin: Diànyǐng lǐ de dòngzuò hěn jīngcǎi.
examples.english: The action in the movie is amazing.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Commonly used for specific moves (in dance, sports) or general action (in movies).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like a baby (巳) wrapped in a blanket (勹) — a wrapped bundle or bag.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted a fetus wrapped in a womb, symbolizing an enclosure or wrapping. The modern meaning extended to bags and the act of wrapping.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yī gè xīn bāo.
examples.english: I bought a new bag.

examples.pinyin: Zhège tàocān bāo wǔfàn ma?
examples.english: Does this set meal include lunch?

vocabulary.usage_notes: As a noun: a bag. As a verb: to wrap, to include, or to guarantee.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 包 (wrap) + 子 (noun suffix). A little wrapped thing. It's wrapped dough with filling inside!
vocabulary.etymology: 包 (to wrap) + 子 (diminutive noun suffix). Literally "little wrapped thing".

examples.pinyin: Zǎocān wǒ chī le liǎng gè bāozi.
examples.english: I ate two steamed buns for breakfast.

examples.chinese: 你喜欢吃什么馅儿的包子？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ xǐhuan chī shénme xiànr de bāozi?
examples.english: What filling do you like in your steamed buns?

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very common Chinese breakfast/snack. The 'zi' is neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Two people (背) back-to-back. Ancient Chinese believed north was where backs faced (the emperor sat facing south).
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph originally representing two people standing back-to-back. In ancient Chinese orientation, the ruler faced south, so his back (北) was to the north.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā zài Běijīng de běibiān.
examples.english: My house is north of Beijing.

examples.pinyin: Dōngtiān běi fēng hěn dà.
examples.english: The north wind is very strong in winter.

vocabulary.usage_notes: One of the four cardinal directions.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 北 (north) + 边 (side). The side that's north.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 北 (north) and 边 (side/edge). Literally "north side".

examples.pinyin: Chāoshì zài wǒ jiā de běibiān.
examples.english: The supermarket is north of my house.

examples.pinyin: Wǎng běibiān zǒu jiù shì huǒchēzhàn.
examples.english: If you go north, you'll reach the train station.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 'bian' is usually neutral tone. Common in giving directions.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 午 (noon) + 饭 (meal). The noon meal.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 午 (noon, 11am-1pm) and 饭 (meal, cooked rice). Literally "noon meal".

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen yīqǐ qù chī wǔfàn ba.
examples.english: Let's go eat lunch together.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jīntiān wǔfàn chī le shénme?
examples.english: What did you eat for lunch today?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Synonymous with 中饭.

vocabulary.english: half a day / a long time
vocabulary.mnemonic: 半 (half) + 天 (day). Half of the sky/day.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 半 (half) and 天 (day/sky). Literally "half a day".

examples.pinyin: Wǒ děng le nǐ bàntiān!
examples.english: I've been waiting for you for ages!

examples.chinese: 这件事我做了半天才做完。
examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì wǒ zuò le bàntiān cái zuò wán.
examples.english: It took me half a day/a long time to finish this.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used colloquially to exaggerate the length of time, meaning "a really long time".

vocabulary.mnemonic: 半 (half) + 年 (year). Half a year.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 半 (half) and 年 (year). Literally "half a year".

examples.pinyin: Wǒ lái Zhōngguó bànnián le.
examples.english: I've been in China for half a year.

examples.pinyin: Zhè fèn hétong qiān bànnián.
examples.english: This contract is for half a year.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A precise time expression. Does not carry the exaggerated "a long time" meaning like 半天 might.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of a plant growing toward the sunny south (ancient pictogram may have depicted a hanging percussion instrument facing south in rituals).
vocabulary.etymology: The character's origin is debated. Some link it to a pictogram of a hanging drum or bell used in southern-facing ceremonies, leading to its association with the south.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā chuānghu cháo nán.
examples.english: My house windows face south.

examples.pinyin: Hǎinán zài Zhōngguó de nánbian.
examples.english: Hainan is in the south of China.

vocabulary.usage_notes: One of the four cardinal directions.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 南 (south) + 边 (side). The side that's south.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 南 (south) and 边 (side/edge). Literally "south side".

examples.pinyin: Xuéxiào zài yīyuàn de nánbian.
examples.english: The school is south of the hospital.

examples.pinyin: Cóng zhèr wǎng nánbian zǒu.
examples.english: Go south from here.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 'bian' is usually neutral tone. Common in giving directions.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 去 (go/past) + 年 (year). The year that went past.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 去 (to go) and 年 (year). Literally "the gone year" or "past year".

examples.pinyin: Wǒ qùnián dàxué bìyè.
examples.english: I graduated from university last year.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ qùnián zài nǎr gōngzuò?
examples.english: Where did you work last year?

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like a square mouth or an open doorway.
vocabulary.etymology: A pictogram of an open mouth. It is one of the simplest and oldest Chinese characters.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kǒu kě le.
examples.english: I'm thirsty. (Mouth is dry)

examples.pinyin: Xuéxiào ménkǒu jiàn.
examples.english: See you at the school gate.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Also used as a measure word for things related to mouths (people, pigs) or things with openings (wells, jars).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A hand (又) helping from the side (口). In ancient times, the right hand was the helping/strong hand.
vocabulary.etymology: Composed of 口 (mouth) and 又 (hand). May represent the right hand bringing food to the mouth, as most people are right-handed.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng wǎng yòu zhuǎn.
examples.english: Please turn right.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de yòushǒu shòushāng le.
examples.english: My right hand is injured.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to the right side. 右手 (yòushǒu) means right hand.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 右 (right) + 边 (side). The side that's right.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 右 (right) and 边 (side/edge). Literally "right side".

examples.pinyin: Yàoshi zài zhuōzi de yòubian.
examples.english: The keys are on the right side of the table.

examples.pinyin: Zài nǐ yòubian yǒu yī jiā yínháng.
examples.english: There's a bank on your right.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 'bian' is usually neutral tone. Common in giving directions.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 吃 (eat) + 饭 (rice/meal). To eat the meal.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 吃 (to eat) and 饭 (cooked rice/meal). Literally "to eat rice/meal".

examples.pinyin: Nǐ chīfàn le ma?
examples.english: Have you eaten?

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen yīqǐ qù chīfàn ba.
examples.english: Let's go eat together.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The most common and casual way to say "to have a meal". "Have you eaten?" is a common greeting.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 后 (after) + 天 (day). The day after the coming day (tomorrow).
vocabulary.etymology: Traditional form 後天 is a compound of 後 (after/behind) and 天 (day). Literally "the day after".

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen hòutiān qù páshān ba.
examples.english: Let's go hiking the day after tomorrow.

examples.pinyin: Huìyì gǎi dào hòutiān le.
examples.english: The meeting has been changed to the day after tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Note the simplified/traditional difference: 后天 (simplified for 'day after tomorrow') vs 後天 (traditional).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 后 (back/behind) + 边 (side). The side that's behind.
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 後邊, a compound of 後 (behind/after) and 边 (side/edge). Literally "back side".

examples.pinyin: Tā zuò zài wǒ hòubian.
examples.english: He sits behind me.

examples.chinese: 房子的后边有一个花园。
examples.pinyin: Fángzi de hòubian yǒu yī gè huāyuán.
examples.english: There is a garden behind the house.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 'bian' is usually neutral tone. Common in giving locations.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think of the sound "ba" as a gentle nudge at the end of a sentence.
vocabulary.etymology: A phonetic loan character. Originally represented a place where wine/drinks were sold (酒吧). Now used for its sound as a modal particle.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen zǒu ba.
examples.english: Let's go.

examples.pinyin: Zhèyàng yīnggāi kěyǐ ba.
examples.english: This should be okay, right?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used at the end of a sentence to: 1) make a suggestion (soft command), 2) seek agreement or confirmation, 3) soften a statement.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 听 (listen) + 写 (write). You listen and then write.
vocabulary.etymology: A compound of 听 (to listen) and 写 (to write). Literally "listen-write".

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān yǒu Zhōngwén tīngxiě.
examples.english: We have a Chinese dictation tomorrow.

examples.chinese: 老师正在给我们听写生词。
examples.pinyin: Lǎoshī zhèngzài gěi wǒmen tīngxiě shēngcí.
examples.english: The teacher is dictating new vocabulary to us.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A common classroom activity where a teacher reads words/text and students write them down.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Imagine GAN JING sounds like 'gone germs' after you clean.
vocabulary.etymology: 干 (dry, shield) + 净 (clean, pure). Combined meaning suggests being free from dirt.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge fáng jiān hěn gān jìng.
examples.english: This room is very clean.

examples.pinyin: Bǎ shǒu xǐ gān jìng zài chī fàn.
examples.english: Wash your hands clean before eating.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used to describe places or objects. Can also mean 'finished/completely' in casual speech (e.g., 吃干净 - eat it all up).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like a wooden bed frame with a mattress (广) and legs (木).
vocabulary.etymology: Originally pictographic of a piece of furniture for sleeping. The modern form contains 木 (wood).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ lèi le, xiǎng shàng chuáng shuì jiào.
examples.english: I'm tired, I want to go to bed.

examples.pinyin: Tā de chuáng hěn dà.
examples.english: His bed is very big.

vocabulary.english: to open; to drive; to turn on
vocabulary.mnemonic: KAI (开) sounds like the 'kye' in 'sky' opening up. The character resembles two hands opening a gate.
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 開, which originally depicted two hands opening a bolt on a door gate.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng kāi mén.
examples.english: Please open the door.

examples.pinyin: Kāi dēng, tài àn le.
examples.english: Turn on the light, it's too dark.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Extremely versatile verb. Basic meaning is 'to open' or 'to start'. It's used in many compounds (开车, 开会, 开玩笑).

vocabulary.mnemonic: KAI (open) + HUI (meeting) = open a meeting.
vocabulary.etymology: 开 (to open/start) + 会 (meeting/gathering).

examples.pinyin: Jīng lǐ zài kāi huì, qǐng děng yī xià.
examples.english: The manager is in a meeting, please wait a moment.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men xià wǔ sān diǎn kāi huì.
examples.english: We are having a meeting at 3 pm.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used with 在 to indicate someone is currently in a meeting.

vocabulary.mnemonic: KAI (open) + WAN (play) + XIAO (laugh) = open up play and laughter.
vocabulary.etymology: 开 (to open/start) + 玩 (to play) + 笑 (to laugh). Literally 'to open play and laughter'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shì kāi wán xiào de, bié shēng qì!
examples.english: I was joking, don't be angry!

examples.pinyin: Tā xǐ huān gēn péng you kāi wán xiào.
examples.english: He likes to joke with his friends.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very common phrase. Can be used as a verb phrase or a noun (e.g., 别开玩笑了! - Don't joke!).

vocabulary.mnemonic: KAI (open/operate) + CHE (vehicle) = operate a vehicle.
vocabulary.etymology: 开 (to operate/start) + 车 (vehicle).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bà ba měi tiān kāi chē shàng bān.
examples.english: My dad drives to work every day.

examples.pinyin: Hē le jiǔ bú yào kāi chē.
examples.english: Don't drive after drinking.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The general verb for driving any car or vehicle. For riding a bike, use 骑自行车.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character DI (弟) looks like a younger brother holding a bow (弓) under an older brother's authority (丷).
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted a sequence or order,引申为 younger male in the family order.

measure_word.example: 一个弟弟 (yī gè dì di)

examples.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ dì.
examples.english: He is my younger brother.

examples.pinyin: Dì, guò lái yī xià.
examples.english: Little brother, come here for a sec.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used alone as a form of address within the family. More commonly used in the reduplicated form 弟弟 in modern Mandarin.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Repeat DI to make it sound cuter and more affectionate, like a little brother.
vocabulary.etymology: Reduplication of 弟 (younger brother), common in Chinese for kinship terms.

measure_word.example: 一个弟弟 (yī gè dì di)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de dì di wǔ suì le.
examples.english: My younger brother is five years old.

examples.pinyin: Dì di zài fáng jiān lǐ wán.
examples.english: Little brother is playing in the room.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The standard, more common term than单用 弟. The second 弟 is neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: DE (virtue/得) + DAO (arrive/到) = virtue arrives → you get something.
vocabulary.etymology: 得 (to get) + 到 (to arrive). Together they emphasize the successful attainment of something.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ dé dào le yī gè xīn gōng zuò.
examples.english: I got a new job.

examples.pinyin: Nǔ lì jiù huì dé dào hǎo chéng jī.
examples.english: If you work hard, you'll get good grades.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used for abstract things like opportunities, results, permission, or answers. More formal than 拿 for physical objects.

vocabulary.mnemonic: WANG (忘) sounds like 'wrong' - you forget things when your memory goes wrong. Heart (心) under 'dead' (亡) = dead heart to memory.
vocabulary.etymology: 亡 (to die/lose) + 心 (heart). Losing something from the heart/mind.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ wàng dài shǒu jī le.
examples.english: I forgot to bring my phone.

examples.pinyin: Bié wàng le wǒ.
examples.english: Don't forget me.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often followed by a verb or an object. Commonly used in its compound form 忘记.

vocabulary.mnemonic: WANG (forget) + JI (remember) = forget to remember.
vocabulary.etymology: 忘 (to forget) + 记 (to remember). An ironic compound meaning the opposite of 'remember'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ wàng jì le tā de míng zi.
examples.english: I forgot his name.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào wàng jì míng tiān kāi huì.
examples.english: Please don't forget the meeting tomorrow.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Slightly more formal and complete than单用 忘, but both are common in speech.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Heart (忄) +亡 (to die) = your heart is dead because you're so busy.
vocabulary.etymology: 忄(heart/mind) + 亡 (to lose/perish). A heart lost in tasks.

examples.pinyin: Zuì jìn gōng zuò hěn máng.
examples.english: Work has been very busy lately.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zài máng shén me?
examples.english: What are you busy with?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can be used as a stative verb (我很忙) or an action verb (在忙工作).

vocabulary.mnemonic: It's 你 (you) with a 心 (heart) underneath, showing you speak from the heart with respect.
vocabulary.etymology: 你 (you) + 心 (heart) → a 'you' spoken from the heart, indicating respect.

examples.pinyin: Nín hǎo, qǐng wèn xū yào bāng zhù ma?
examples.english: Hello (polite), do you need help?

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì gěi nín de lǐ wù.
examples.english: This is a gift for you.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for elders, superiors, or customers to show respect. Not used among close friends or family.

vocabulary.mnemonic: WO (I) + MEN (plural marker) = I + others = we.
vocabulary.etymology: 我 (I) + 们 (plural suffix for pronouns and some nouns).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men shì xué sheng.
examples.english: We are students.

examples.chinese: 周末我们一起去看电影吧。
examples.pinyin: Zhōu mò wǒ men yī qǐ qù kàn diàn yǐng ba.
examples.english: Let's go see a movie together this weekend.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The standard word for 'we'. 咱们 (zán men) is more inclusive, implying 'you and I'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: FANG (house) + ZI (noun suffix) = a house thing.
vocabulary.etymology: 房 (house/room) + 子 (noun suffix indicating a concrete object).

measure_word.example: 一套房子 (yī tào fáng zi)

examples.pinyin: Tā men mǎi le yī gè xīn fáng zi.
examples.english: They bought a new house.

examples.pinyin: Zhè zuò fáng zi hěn piào liang.
examples.english: This house is very beautiful.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to the physical building. 家 (jiā) often means 'home' or 'family'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: FANG (house) + JIAN (space between) = the space inside a house.
vocabulary.etymology: 房 (house) + 间 (interval/space between). A space within a house.

measure_word.example: 一个房间 (yī gè fáng jiān)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de fáng jiān yǒu diǎn luàn.
examples.english: My room is a bit messy.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge jiǔ diàn fáng jiān hěn dà.
examples.english: This hotel room is very big.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to any room (bedroom, living room, hotel room).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character SHOU looks like a simplified drawing of a hand with fingers.
vocabulary.etymology: A pictograph of a hand with five fingers.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng jǔ qǐ nǐ de shǒu.
examples.english: Please raise your hand.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shǒu hěn lěng.
examples.english: My hands are very cold.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Also appears in many compounds related to skill or manual action (手机, 手表, 高手).

vocabulary.mnemonic: DA (打) sounds like the 'da' in 'dad' spanking. Hand (扌) +丁 (nail) = hitting a nail.
vocabulary.etymology: 扌(hand) + 丁 (nail). Originally meant to strike, like hammering a nail.

examples.pinyin: Bú yào dǎ rén.
examples.english: Don't hit people.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài dǎ diàn huà.
examples.english: I'm making a phone call.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A 'light verb' with dozens of meanings depending on the object (打电话, 打球, 打车, 打字). Core idea is 'to perform an action (often involving contact)'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: DA (hit/do) + KAI (open) = do the opening.
vocabulary.etymology: 打 (to do/hit) + 开 (to open). A verb-complement compound.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bāng wǒ dǎ kāi chuāng hu.
examples.english: Please help me open the window.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ dǎ bù kāi zhè ge píng zi.
examples.english: I can't open this bottle.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used for opening physical objects (boxes, windows, bottles). More specific than 开 alone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: DA (hit/play) + QIU (ball) = hit/play the ball.
vocabulary.etymology: 打 (to hit) + 球 (ball).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ péng you xǐ huān dǎ qiú.
examples.english: My friend likes to play ball sports.

examples.pinyin: Xià wǔ wǒ men qù dǎ qiú ba.
examples.english: Let's go play ball this afternoon.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A general term for playing any sport with a ball. Specify with 打篮球, 打网球, etc.

vocabulary.mnemonic: DA (call/do) + CHE (vehicle) = call for a vehicle.
vocabulary.etymology: 打 (to call/hail) + 车 (vehicle). Originally from hailing a rickshaw or car.

examples.pinyin: Xià yǔ le, wǒ men dǎ chē ba.
examples.english: It's raining, let's take a taxi.

examples.chinese: 从这里打车去机场很贵。
examples.pinyin: Cóng zhè lǐ dǎ chē qù jī chǎng hěn guì.
examples.english: Taking a taxi to the airport from here is expensive.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The standard casual phrase. Equivalent to 坐出租车.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Hand (扌) + a sword/ dagger (戈) = using your hand and a tool to search thoroughly.
vocabulary.etymology: 扌(hand) + 戈 (dagger-axe). Possibly suggesting searching by hand and weapon (to clear obstacles).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài zhǎo wǒ de yào shi.
examples.english: I'm looking for my keys.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zhǎo dào gōng zuò le ma?
examples.english: Have you found a job?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Means 'to look for'. When combined with 到 (zhǎo dào), it means 'to have found'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: ZHAO (look for) + DAO (arrive) = the search has arrived at its target.
vocabulary.etymology: 找 (to look for) + 到 (to arrive/reach). A verb-complement compound indicating successful completion.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zhōng yú zhǎo dào nǐ le!
examples.english: I finally found you!

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zhǎo dào nà jiā cān tīng le ma?
examples.english: Did you find that restaurant?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Indicates the action of searching is complete and successful. 找 alone is the process.

vocabulary.english: to take; to hold; to get
vocabulary.mnemonic: NA (拿) sounds like 'nah, I'll take it'. Hand (手) + 合 (to combine) = hand combines with an object.
vocabulary.etymology: 手 (hand) + 合 (to combine/unite). A hand uniting with an object to hold it.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng ná yī bēi shuǐ gěi wǒ.
examples.english: Please get a glass of water for me.

examples.pinyin: Tā shǒu lǐ ná zhe shǒu jī.
examples.english: He is holding a phone in his hand.

vocabulary.usage_notes: For physically taking/holding objects. Also used in 拿出来 (take out), 拿过来 (bring over).

vocabulary.mnemonic: FANG (put/let go) + JIA (holiday) = let go of work for a holiday.
vocabulary.etymology: 放 (to put/let go) + 假 (holiday/leave). To be given leave from work/school.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ men xià xīng qī fàng jià.
examples.english: We have a holiday next week.

examples.pinyin: Fàng jià le nǐ dǎ suàn zuò shén me?
examples.english: What do you plan to do during the holiday?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used for institutional holidays (school, company). The subject is usually the person/group enjoying the break.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A little child with arms outstretched.
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph of an infant with arms swaddled. Now also a common noun suffix.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge hái zi hěn cōng míng.
examples.english: This child is very smart.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào yī gè bēi zi.
examples.english: I want a cup.

vocabulary.usage_notes: As a suffix, makes nouns out of other words (e.g., 桌 table -> 桌子 desk).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A baby (子) under a roof (宀) learning characters.
vocabulary.etymology: 宀 (roof) + 子 (child). Suggests a child being educated at home.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ rèn shí zhè gè zì ma?
examples.english: Do you know this character?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de míng zì shì sān gè zì.
examples.english: My name is three characters long.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers specifically to Chinese characters, not general 'words'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A child (子) under a roof (宀) practicing with hands (扌) -> studying.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted hands (臼 variant) arranging counting rods, with 子 (child) added later. Simplified form uses 子.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài xué Zhōng wén.
examples.english: I am learning Chinese.

examples.pinyin: Tā hěn xǐ huān xué.
examples.english: He really likes to study.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used as a verb. Can be a noun meaning 'school' or 'study field'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The place (院) where you learn (学).
vocabulary.etymology: 学 (study) + 院 (courtyard, compound). A compound meaning a place of advanced learning.

measure_word.example: 一所学院 (yī suǒ xué yuàn)

examples.pinyin: Tā zài yī xué yuàn xué xí.
examples.english: He studies at the medical college.

examples.pinyin: Zhè gè xué yuàn hěn dà.
examples.english: This college is very big.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A specialized part of a university (e.g., College of Arts) or a standalone institute.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A small child (子) who is still a youth (孩).
vocabulary.etymology: 孩 originally meant 'to laugh like a child'. Combined with 子 (child) for emphasis.

measure_word.example: 一个孩子 (yī gè hái zi)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng gè hái zi.
examples.english: My family has two kids.

examples.pinyin: Nà hái zi zhēn kě ài.
examples.english: That child is really cute.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Common and neutral term for children. The '子' is a suffix and is neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The people (人) in your home (家).
vocabulary.etymology: 家 (home/family) + 人 (person). A compound literally meaning 'home people'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de jiā rén dōu zài Běi jīng.
examples.english: All my family members are in Beijing.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hé jiā rén yī qǐ chī fàn.
examples.english: I eat with my family.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to immediate family members collectively. Often used as '我的家人'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Inside (里) the home (家).
vocabulary.etymology: 家 (home) + 里 (inside). A compound indicating location inside the home/family sphere.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lǐ yǒu sān gè rén.
examples.english: There are three people in my home.

examples.pinyin: Tā zài jiā lǐ gōng zuò.
examples.english: He works at home.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used to indicate location (at home) or the domestic sphere (within the family).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A hand (又) holding a measuring tool (寸) to check if something is RIGHT.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted a hand holding an ancient measuring tool, implying comparison and correctness.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ shuō de hěn duì.
examples.english: What you said is very right.

examples.pinyin: Tā duì wǒ shuō “nǐ hǎo”.
examples.english: He said 'hello' to me.

vocabulary.usage_notes: As a preposition (对...), it marks the target or recipient of an action.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A single stroke hanging down, like something tiny.
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph of three small particles or grains, representing something tiny.

examples.pinyin: Zhè gè fáng zi hěn xiǎo.
examples.english: This house is very small.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mèi mei hái xiǎo.
examples.english: My younger sister is still young.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Opposite of 大 (big). Often used as a prefix for things that are small or junior.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The school (学) for small (小) kids.
vocabulary.etymology: 小 (small/young) + 学 (school). A compound for the school level for young children.

measure_word.example: 一所小学 (yī suǒ xiǎo xué)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ nǚ ér zài shàng xiǎo xué.
examples.english: My daughter is in primary school.

examples.pinyin: Xiǎo xué jiù zài wǒ jiā páng biān.
examples.english: The elementary school is right next to my house.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to grades 1-6 in the Chinese system.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A student (生) of the small (小) school (学).
vocabulary.etymology: 小学 (primary school) + 生 (life, student). A compound meaning 'primary school life/student'.

measure_word.example: 一个小学生 (yī gè xiǎo xué shēng)

examples.pinyin: Zhè xiē xiǎo xué shēng hěn kě ài.
examples.english: These primary school pupils are very cute.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ dì di shì xiǎo xué shēng.
examples.english: My younger brother is a primary school student.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Specifically refers to a student enrolled in 小学.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A small (小) child (孩) with an 'er' sound for cuteness.
vocabulary.etymology: 小 (small) + 孩 (child) + 儿 (erhua suffix). The '儿' adds a colloquial, often northern, flavor.

measure_word.example: 一个小孩儿 (yī gè xiǎo hái r)

examples.pinyin: Gōng yuán lǐ yǒu hěn duō xiǎo hái r.
examples.english: There are many kids in the park.

examples.pinyin: Nà gè xiǎo hái r pǎo de zhēn kuài!
examples.english: That kid runs really fast!

vocabulary.usage_notes: Very common in spoken Mandarin, especially in northern China. The '儿' is fused, not a separate syllable.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A small (小) friend (朋友) you play with.
vocabulary.etymology: 小 (small/little) + 朋友 (friend). A term for a child, emphasizing their friendliness.

measure_word.example: 一个小朋友 (yī gè xiǎo péng yǒu)

examples.pinyin: Xiǎo péng yǒu men, kuài lái wán ba!
examples.english: Kids, come and play!

examples.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ de xiǎo péng yǒu.
examples.english: She is my little friend (a kid I know).

vocabulary.usage_notes: A warm, polite way to address or refer to children, often used by adults or teachers.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A few (少) small (小) drops missing a stroke.
vocabulary.etymology: Derived from 小 (small). The additional stroke suggests reducing or making smaller.

examples.pinyin: Zhè lǐ rén hěn shǎo.
examples.english: There are very few people here.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng shǎo fàng diǎn táng.
examples.english: Please put in less sugar.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Opposite of 多 (many/much). Can be used before verbs to mean 'do less of something'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A bird (京 variant) on a high place, indicating immediacy or precision.
vocabulary.etymology: Complex evolution. One theory links it to a character meaning 'high', suggesting reaching a point promptly.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiù lái.
examples.english: I'm coming right now.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiù shì wǒ de jiā.
examples.english: This is exactly my home.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very common adverb emphasizing immediacy, precision, or used in conditional sentences (如果...就...).

vocabulary.mnemonic: Looks like a mountain with three peaks.
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph of a mountain range with peaks.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xǐ huān pá shān.
examples.english: I like to climb mountains.

examples.pinyin: Nà zuò shān hěn gāo.
examples.english: That mountain is very high.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very basic and common character for geographical features.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The sun (日) walks (步) as time passes for another year of age.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally written with 步 (walk) and 戌 (a weapon), later simplified. Conveys the passing of time.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jǐ suì le?
examples.english: How old are you? (for kids)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ èr shí suì.
examples.english: I am twenty years old.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used exclusively for expressing age. The measure word is integrated (几岁, 二十岁).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A person (人) who works (工).
vocabulary.etymology: 工 (work/labor) + 人 (person). A straightforward compound.

measure_word.example: 一个工人 (yī gè gōng rén)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bà ba shì gōng rén.
examples.english: My dad is a worker.

examples.pinyin: Gōng rén men zài xiū lù.
examples.english: The workers are repairing the road.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A general term for blue-collar or manual workers.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A hand (ナ/手 variant) holding a tool (工), traditionally the assisting (left) hand.
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph of a left hand. The modern form is a simplification.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng wǎng zuǒ zǒu.
examples.english: Please go left.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yòng zuǒ shǒu xiě zì.
examples.english: I write with my left hand.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Opposite of 右 (right). Often used in directional phrases.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The side (边) that is left (左).
vocabulary.etymology: 左 (left) + 边 (side). A compound specifying location.

examples.pinyin: Yín háng zài zuǒ bian.
examples.english: The bank is on the left side.

examples.pinyin: Zuò zài wǒ zuǒ bian.
examples.english: Sit on my left.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The '边' here is often in the neutral tone (bian). Used for indicating location.

vocabulary.english: poor; bad; to differ; to lack
vocabulary.mnemonic: A hand (左 variant) working with wool (工 + 丿) -> tangled and messy, hence poor quality.
vocabulary.etymology: Complex. One interpretation involves hands and wool, implying disorder or discrepancy.

examples.pinyin: Tā de chéng jī hěn chà.
examples.english: His grades are very poor.

examples.pinyin: Hái chà shí kuài qián.
examples.english: It's still short by ten kuai.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Read as 'chà' for 'poor/bad/lacking'. Read as 'chā' for 'difference' (less common in daily speech).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A helping hand (邦, phonetic) giving cloth (巾) as aid.
vocabulary.etymology: 巾 (cloth) + 邦 (phonetic). Cloth was used for binding and aiding.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ néng bāng wǒ ma?
examples.english: Can you help me?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ lái bāng nǐ ná.
examples.english: Let me help you carry it.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Very common in casual speech. Often used in the phrase '帮(一)个忙' (do a favor).

vocabulary.mnemonic: A towel (巾) in a house (宀) -> a daily, regular item.
vocabulary.etymology: 尚 (phonetic/meaning 'still, yet') + 巾 (towel/cloth). Conveys regularity or commonness.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ cháng qù nà jiā kā fēi diàn.
examples.english: I often go to that café.

examples.pinyin: Tā cháng cháng chí dào.
examples.english: He is often late.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can be doubled as 常常 for extra emphasis on frequency.

vocabulary.mnemonic: A shield (干 ancient form) in the sun -> dry.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally a pictograph of a shield. The meaning 'dry' is a phonetic loan.

examples.pinyin: Yī fu gān le.
examples.english: The clothes are dry.

examples.pinyin: Jīn tiān tiān qì hěn gān.
examples.english: The weather is very dry today.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Read as 'gān' for 'dry'. Distinguish from 干 (gàn) meaning 'to do'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Doing (干) what (什么) thing?
vocabulary.etymology: 干 (to do) + 什么 (what). A literal compound.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zài gàn shén me?
examples.english: What are you doing?

examples.pinyin: Nǐ gàn shén me shēng qì?
examples.english: Why are you angry? (colloquial)

vocabulary.usage_notes: Extremely common in spoken Chinese. Can be used to ask about an action or the reason for it.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 坐 (zuò) sounds like 'z' and you need to 'zit' down!
vocabulary.etymology: 坐 depicts two people sitting on the ground (土). 下 indicates the direction/downward action.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ lèi le, kuài zuò xia ba.
examples.english: You're tired, sit down quickly.

examples.chinese: 大家都坐下，我们开始开会。
examples.pinyin: Dàjiā dōu zuò xia, wǒmen kāishǐ kāihuì.
examples.english: Everyone sit down, we're starting the meeting.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used as a command or suggestion. 下 is in the neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 外 (wài) means outside. 外国 is the country outside yours.
vocabulary.etymology: 外 originally meant outside/outer. 国 (simplified from 國) depicts a walled territory. Combined meaning 'outer territory'.

measure_word.example: 一个外国 (yī gè wài guó)

examples.chinese: 我朋友要去外国工作了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ péngyou yào qù wài guó gōngzuò le.
examples.english: My friend is going to work in a foreign country.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge cài shì wài guó cài.
examples.english: This dish is foreign cuisine.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to a country, not a language.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 外 (outside) + 语 (language) = a language from outside.
vocabulary.etymology: 外 (outside/foreign). 语 (simplified from 語) means speech/language.

measure_word.example: 一门外语 (yī mén wài yǔ)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ huì shuō sān mén wài yǔ.
examples.english: I can speak three foreign languages.

examples.pinyin: Xué wài yǔ hěn yǒu yìsi.
examples.english: Learning a foreign language is very interesting.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Common measure word is 门 for academic subjects.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 外边 is the 'outside border' (边) of something.
vocabulary.etymology: 外 (outside). 边 (simplified from 邊) means side/border.

examples.pinyin: Wài bian zài xià yǔ, dài bǎ sǎn.
examples.english: It's raining outside, take an umbrella.

examples.chinese: 孩子们都在外边玩儿呢。
examples.pinyin: Háizimen dōu zài wài bian wánr ne.
examples.english: The kids are all playing outside.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often interchangeable with 外面. 边 is in the neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Picture two 夕 (evenings) stacked up, meaning many nights.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted two pieces of meat, suggesting duplication/abundance, which evolved to mean many/much.

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān chāoshì rén hǎo duō a.
examples.english: There are so many people at the supermarket today.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ duō dà le?
examples.english: How old are you?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can be an adjective ('many things') or an adverb in questions ('how...?').

vocabulary.mnemonic: Looks like a person (人) with arms outstretched, showing how big something is.
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph of a person with arms and legs spread out, emphasizing size.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge fángzi zhēn dà!
examples.english: This house is really big!

examples.pinyin: Tā bǐ wǒ dà liǎng suì.
examples.english: He is two years older than me.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Also used for age (older) and volume (loud). Opposite is 小.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 大 (big) + 学 (learning) = the big school.
vocabulary.etymology: 大 (great). 学 (simplified from 學) means to learn/study. 'Great learning' or 'higher education'.

measure_word.example: 一所大学 (yī suǒ dà xué)

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mèimei míngnián shàng dà xué.
examples.english: My younger sister will go to university next year.

examples.pinyin: Běijīng Dàxué hěn yǒumíng.
examples.english: Peking University is very famous.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used as part of a proper name (e.g., 清华大学).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 大学 (university) + 生 (life/living being) = person living the university life.
vocabulary.etymology: 大学 (university) + 生 (born, life, person).

measure_word.example: 一个大学生 (yī gè dà xué shēng)

examples.pinyin: Tā shì gè dà xué shēng, hěn máng.
examples.english: He's a university student, very busy.

examples.pinyin: Dà xué shēng kěyǐ bànjià mǎi piào.
examples.english: University students can buy tickets at half price.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 大 (big) with an extra dot, meaning it's gone past big to 'too much'.
vocabulary.etymology: Derived from 大 (big) with an added mark to indicate excess or extremity.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu tài dà le.
examples.english: This piece of clothing is too big.

examples.pinyin: Tài xièxie nǐ le!
examples.english: Thank you so much!

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for emphasis. Often paired with 了 in the pattern '太 + adj. + 了'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Looks like a person kneeling with arms crossed, a traditional posture for women in ancient times.
vocabulary.etymology: Pictograph of a person in a kneeling/submissive posture, representing a woman.

measure_word.example: 一个女人 (yī gè nǚ rén)

examples.chinese: 她是一个很厉害的女医生。
examples.pinyin: Tā shì yī gè hěn lìhai de nǚ yīshēng.
examples.english: She is a very capable female doctor.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge fángjiān shì nǚ cèsuǒ.
examples.english: This room is the women's restroom.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used as a modifier before other nouns (e.g., 女朋友).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 女 (female) + 孩儿 (kid) = a female kid.
vocabulary.etymology: 女 (female). 孩儿 is a colloquial term for child/kid, with 儿化音 (ér-huà yīn).

measure_word.example: 一个女孩儿 (yī gè nǚ háir)

examples.chinese: 那个女孩儿是我妹妹的同学。
examples.pinyin: Nà ge nǚ háir shì wǒ mèimei de tóngxué.
examples.english: That girl is my younger sister's classmate.

examples.chinese: 她小时候是个安静的女孩儿。
examples.pinyin: Tā xiǎo shíhou shì gè ānjìng de nǚ háir.
examples.english: She was a quiet girl when she was little.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The 儿化音 (ér sound) is typical of northern spoken Mandarin.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 女 (female) + 朋友 (friend) = a female friend of a special kind.
vocabulary.etymology: 女 (female). 朋友 means friend.

measure_word.example: 一个女朋友 (yī gè nǚ péngyou)

examples.chinese: 他周末要和女朋友去看电影。
examples.pinyin: Tā zhōumò yào hé nǚ péngyou qù kàn diànyǐng.
examples.english: He's going to the movies with his girlfriend this weekend.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hái méiyǒu nǚ péngyou.
examples.english: I don't have a girlfriend yet.

vocabulary.usage_notes: 朋 and 友 are both in the neutral tone here.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 女 (female) + 生 (student) = a female student.
vocabulary.etymology: 女 (female). 生 (as in 学生, student).

measure_word.example: 一个女生 (yī gè nǚ shēng)

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bān yǒu èrshí gè nǚ shēng.
examples.english: There are twenty female students in our class.

examples.pinyin: Nà ge nǚ shēng chànggē hěn hǎotīng.
examples.english: That girl sings very well.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Common in school contexts. Can also refer to young women casually.

vocabulary.mnemonic: The character looks like a woman (女) with an extra stroke, maybe holding a baby for milk.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally associated with 女 (woman), relating to breastfeeding, later extended to milk in general.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang hē yī bēi nǎi.
examples.english: I drink a glass of milk every morning.

examples.pinyin: Bǎobao yào hē nǎi le.
examples.english: The baby needs to drink milk.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often part of compound words like 牛奶 (cow's milk). Can mean 'breast' or 'breast milk' in certain contexts.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 奶 (milk) repeated, like the one who fed you milk when you were a baby.
vocabulary.etymology: Reduplication of 奶, originally meaning wet nurse or mother, now specifically paternal grandmother.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ nǎinai jīnnián qīshí suì le.
examples.english: My grandmother is seventy years old this year.

examples.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ qù kàn nǎinai.
examples.english: I'm going to see my grandmother this weekend.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A kinship term. The second 奶 is in the neutral tone. Usually refers to father's mother.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 她 (she) + 们 (plural marker) = a group of 'shes'.
vocabulary.etymology: 她 (female she, a modern character) + 们 (plural suffix for people).

examples.pinyin: Tā men dōu shì wǒ de hǎo péngyou.
examples.english: They are all my good friends. (all female)

examples.pinyin: Tā men zài nà bian liáotiān ne.
examples.english: They are chatting over there. (all female)

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used only when the group is exclusively female. For a mixed group, use 他们.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 好 (good) + 吃 (eat) = good to eat.
vocabulary.etymology: 好 (good) + 吃 (to eat). Literally 'good eat'.

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge dàngāo zhēn hǎo chī!
examples.english: This cake is really delicious!

examples.pinyin: Yǒu shénme hǎo chī de cài?
examples.english: What tasty dishes do you have?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Very common compliment for food. 吃 is in the neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 好 (good) + 听 (listen) = good to listen to.
vocabulary.etymology: 好 (good) + 听 (simplified from 聽, to listen/hear).

examples.pinyin: Zhè shǒu gē zhēn hǎo tīng.
examples.english: This song is really nice to listen to.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ de míngzi hěn hǎo tīng.
examples.english: Your name sounds very pleasant.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Used for music, voices, names, etc. Opposite is 难听.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 好 (good) + 玩儿 (to play) = good to play with.
vocabulary.etymology: 好 (good) + 玩儿 (to play, with 儿化音).

examples.pinyin: Zhè ge yóuxì tài hǎo wánr le!
examples.english: This game is so much fun!

examples.chinese: 上海有什么好玩儿的地方？
examples.pinyin: Shànghǎi yǒu shénme hǎo wánr de dìfang?
examples.english: What fun places are there in Shanghai?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Casual, spoken word. The 儿化音 is typical. Can describe places, things, or activities.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 好 (good) + 看 (look) = good to look at.
vocabulary.etymology: 好 (good) + 看 (to look/watch/see).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zhè jiàn xīn yīfu hěn hǎo kàn.
examples.english: Your new clothes look very good.

examples.pinyin: Nà bù diànyǐng hǎo kàn ma?
examples.english: Is that movie good? (Is it worth watching?)

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can describe people, objects, movies, etc. More casual than 漂亮.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 女 (woman) + 马 (horse). Think of a woman who works as hard as a horse – your mom!
vocabulary.etymology: Composed of 女 (woman) and 马 (mǎ, horse) as a phonetic component.

examples.pinyin: Mā, wǒ huí lái le!
examples.english: Mom, I'm home!

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ mā zuò de fàn.
examples.english: This is the food my mom made.

vocabulary.usage_notes: An informal, affectionate term for mother. Often used alone as a form of address.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 女 (female) + 未 (not yet). She's female and 'not yet' as old as you.
vocabulary.etymology: 女 (female) + 未 (wèi, not yet) suggesting younger status.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ mèi bǐ wǒ xiǎo wǔ suì.
examples.english: My younger sister is five years younger than me.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì Xiǎo Lǐ, wǒ mèi.
examples.english: This is Xiao Li, my younger sister.

vocabulary.usage_notes: More formal/standalone than 妹妹. Often used in writing or when specifying relationship.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 妹 (younger sister) said twice, making it cuter and more familiar.
vocabulary.etymology: Reduplication of 妹 (younger sister).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hé wǒ mèimei yīqǐ zhù.
examples.english: I live together with my younger sister.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ mèimei duō dà le?
examples.english: How old is your younger sister?

vocabulary.usage_notes: The most common, casual way to say 'younger sister'. The second 妹 is in the neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 女 (female) + 且 (moreover). She's female and 'moreover' older than you.
vocabulary.etymology: 女 (female) + 且 (qiě, moreover/serve as), possibly phonetic and semantic component indicating seniority.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiě duì wǒ hěn hǎo.
examples.english: My older sister is very good to me.

examples.pinyin: Zhāng jiě, nǐ hǎo!
examples.english: Hello, Sister Zhang! (polite/form of address)

vocabulary.usage_notes: Can be used as a polite title for a slightly older woman (e.g., 王姐).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 姐 (older sister) said twice, like calling her name affectionately.
vocabulary.etymology: Reduplication of 姐 (older sister).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiějie huì kāi chē.
examples.english: My older sister can drive.

examples.pinyin: Jiějie, děng deng wǒ!
examples.english: Older sister, wait for me!

vocabulary.usage_notes: The most common, casual way to say 'older sister'. The second 姐 is in the neutral tone.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Think '没 (no) 什么 (what)' = 'It's no big thing!'
vocabulary.etymology: 没 (méi, not have) + 什么 (shénme, what). Literally 'not have what'.

examples.chinese: A: 谢谢你！ B: 没什么。
examples.pinyin: A: Xièxie nǐ! B: Méi shénme.
examples.english: A: Thank you! B: It's nothing.

examples.pinyin: Méi shénme dà wèntí.
examples.english: It's no big problem.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A very common, casual response to thanks or apologies. Used to downplay something.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 没 (mei) sounds like 'may', but here it's 'may NOT have'.
vocabulary.etymology: 没 (méi, not have; originally depicted water covering something) + 有 (yǒu, to have).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ méiyǒu qián.
examples.english: I don't have money.

examples.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu lái.
examples.english: He didn't come.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Negates nouns (don't have) and past actions (did not do). For present/future negation of verbs, use 不 (bù).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The left part (氵) is water, the right part (先) looks like someone bending over a sink.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally showed water (氵) and a foot (足 variant), implying washing feet. Later simplified.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào xǐ yīfu.
examples.english: I want to wash clothes.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xǐ shǒu le ma?
examples.english: Did you wash your hands?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Often used before the object being washed: 洗车 (wash car), 洗碗 (wash dishes).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 洗手 (wash hands) + 间 (room) = the room where you wash your hands.
vocabulary.etymology: 洗 (xǐ, wash) + 手 (shǒu, hand) + 间 (jiān, room).

examples.pinyin: Qǐngwèn, xǐshǒujiān zài nǎr?
examples.english: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ qù yíxià xǐshǒujiān.
examples.english: I'm going to the restroom for a moment.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A polite and common term for public or guest bathrooms. More formal than 厕所.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 火 (fire) + 车 (vehicle) = old 'fire vehicle' (steam train).
vocabulary.etymology: 火 (huǒ, fire) + 车 (chē, vehicle). Reflects steam-powered trains.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen zuò huǒchē qù Běijīng.
examples.english: We are taking the train to Beijing.

examples.pinyin: Huǒchē wǎndiǎn le.
examples.english: The train is delayed.

vocabulary.usage_notes: General term for train. 高铁 (gāotiě) is specifically high-speed rail.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 火车 (train) + 站 (station) = where the train stops.
vocabulary.etymology: 火车 (huǒchē, train) + 站 (zhàn, station; originally meant to stand/stop).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài huǒchēzhàn děng nǐ.
examples.english: I'll wait for you at the train station.

examples.pinyin: Huǒchēzhàn rén hěn duō.
examples.english: The train station is very crowded.

vocabulary.usage_notes: The central hub for train travel. 站 (zhàn) is used for many transport stations.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Left side (执) gives the sound 'rè', imagine someone holding (执) a fireball (灬).
vocabulary.etymology: Simplified from 熱. The bottom component (灬) is the 'fire' radical.

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān tài rè le.
examples.english: Today is too hot.

examples.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn, shuǐ hěn rè!
examples.english: Be careful, the water is very hot!

vocabulary.usage_notes: Describes weather, objects, food, or feelings (热情, enthusiastic). Opposite is 冷 (lěng, cold).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 爱 (love) + 好 (good/liking) = loving something good is a hobby.
vocabulary.etymology: 爱 (ài, love) + 好 (hào, to like).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ de àihào shì shénme?
examples.english: What is your hobby?

examples.pinyin: Tā àihào dǎ lánqiú.
examples.english: He likes playing basketball (as a hobby).

vocabulary.usage_notes: As a noun: 'hobby'. As a verb: 'to be fond of (an activity)'. It's more sustained than just 喜欢.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 爷 (yé) sounds like 'yeah!'—what a grandpa might say. Repeating it makes it affectionate.
vocabulary.etymology: A reduplication of 爷 (yé), an old term for father or elder. Used for paternal grandfather.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yéye jīnnián bāshí suì.
examples.english: My grandfather is eighty years old this year.

examples.pinyin: Yéye, gěi wǒ jiǎng gè gùshi ba!
examples.english: Grandpa, tell me a story!

vocabulary.usage_notes: Informal, affectionate term for father's father. Maternal grandfather is 外公 (wàigōng).

vocabulary.mnemonic: The top (父) means 'father', the bottom (巴) gives the sound 'ba'. Think 'Ba-ba' (dad).
vocabulary.etymology: A phonetic-phonetic compound: 父 (fù, father) for meaning + 巴 (bā) for sound.

examples.pinyin: Bà, wǒ huílai le!
examples.english: Dad, I'm home!

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ bà.
examples.english: This is my dad.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Extremely common, casual term for father. Often used alone or doubled as 爸爸 (bàba).

vocabulary.mnemonic: 玩 (wán) means play, 儿 (ér) is a Beijing accent ending — imagine a kid saying '玩儿去喽!'
vocabulary.etymology: 玩 (wán, to play) + 儿 (ér, colloquial northern suffix). The standard form is 玩.

examples.pinyin: Háizimen zài gōngyuán wánr.
examples.english: The kids are playing in the park.

examples.pinyin: Zhōumò nǐ xiǎng qù nǎr wánr?
examples.english: Where do you want to go have fun this weekend?

vocabulary.usage_notes: Northern colloquial variant of 玩. Very common in spoken Mandarin. Can mean playing games, traveling for fun, or hanging out.

vocabulary.mnemonic: Two 'kings' (玨, ancient jade) under a 'roof' (刂 variant) — kings in a class? No, think of a group organized under one roof.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally depicted dividing jade (玨) with a knife (刀), implying division into groups.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bān yǒu èrshí gè xuéshēng.
examples.english: There are twenty students in our class.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shàng yèbān.
examples.english: I work the night shift.

vocabulary.usage_notes: A group for work, study, or the military. 上班 (shàng bān) means 'to go to work'.

vocabulary.mnemonic: 左 (王) is jade, right (求) sounds like 'qiu' — a precious jade ball.
vocabulary.etymology: Originally meant a type of jade. The 'jade' radical (王) was later replaced by 'jade' (玉) in the traditional form 球.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen qù tī qiú ba!
examples.english: Let's go play soccer (kick the ball)!

examples.pinyin: Zhège qiú shì yuán de.
examples.english: This ball is round.

vocabulary.usage_notes: Refers to any ball or spherical object. Often combined for specific sports: 篮球 (lánqiú, basketball).

vocabulary.english: to get sick / to fall ill
vocabulary.mnemonic: 生 (generate) + 病 (illness) = illness is generated.
vocabulary.etymology: 生 (shēng, to produce) + 病 (bìng, illness/disease).

examples.pinyin: Tā shēngbìng le, jīntiān méi lái.
examples.english: He got sick and didn't come today.

examples.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn bié shēngbìng.
